A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.
PD-1 helps regulate T-cell responses. Blocking its signals can improve cancer control in studied settings, but it does not guarantee recognition, killing or benefit.

PD-L1 and PD-L2 can engage PD-1 on T cells and inhibit proliferation and cytokine production. Pembrolizumab binds PD-1 and blocks its interactions with both ligands. Interrupting this pathway does not supply every other requirement for target recognition, tissue access or useful killing. The U.S. label warns that immune-mediated reactions can be severe or fatal and affect any organ system, including after treatment stops; antitumour activity and safety are separate questions.

Perou and colleagues profiled 65 surgical specimens from 42 patients on cDNA microarrays of 8,102 genes and found the tumours could be classified into subtypes distinguished by pervasive differences in gene expression, the origin of the intrinsic subtypes luminal A, luminal B, HER2-enriched, basal-like and normal-like (Perou 2000). The Cancer Genome Atlas integrated copy number, methylation, exome, mRNA, microRNA and protein data across primary breast cancers, confirmed four main classes, found TP53, PIK3CA and GATA3 the only genes mutated in more than 10 percent overall, and showed basal-like tumours share many molecular features with high-grade serous ovarian cancer, implying a related aetiology and similar therapeutic opportunities (TCGA 2012). Triple-negative and basal-like overlap but are not identical: of 412 triple-negative tumours 21.4 percent were non-basal-like, and of 473 basal-like tumours 31.5 percent were not triple-negative; triple-negative tumours classified as luminal or HER2-enriched had expression profiles indistinguishable from their non-triple-negative counterparts, most HER2-enriched triple-negative tumours lacked HER2 amplification, and the authors suggest triple-negative trials stratify by basal-like versus non-basal-like expression (Prat 2013). In the population-based Carolina Breast Cancer Study, using immunohistochemical surrogates (ER, PR and HER2 negative with cytokeratin 5/6 or HER1 positive), basal-like tumours were found in 39 percent of premenopausal African American women against 14 percent of postmenopausal African American and 16 percent of non-African American women; they had more TP53 mutations (44 against 15 percent), higher mitotic index and grade, and among the shortest breast cancer-specific survival (Carey 2006). Basal-like cancers are the typical cancer of BRCA1 carriers, and adenoid cystic carcinoma is a special type of basal-like tumour with an excellent outlook (Ghabach 2010), a reminder that an expression label does not establish a uniform behaviour or exact cell ancestry. PAM50 basal-like and Lehmann BL1/BL2 belong to different classifiers; a PAM50 basal-like call does not by itself assign either Lehmann profile.

evidence.excerpt:
A circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) assay looks for tumour-associated features in a finite sample of cell-free DNA. How much tumour DNA reaches the sampled blood varies between lesions, and recovery, background DNA, the features tracked and the assay's detection limit all shape the call. Imaging measures a defined region through a physical signal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the breast can report contrast enhancement or the volume of enhancing tissue, which is not a direct count of viable cancer cells. The two tests can therefore differ without either being wrong, and neither automatically replaces the other.

They can also share information. In Magbanua and colleagues' pilot of 84 women having neoadjuvant chemotherapy for early breast cancer, ctDNA concentration was correlated with MRI functional tumour volume at all four time points, with Spearman correlations of 0.42 to 0.49, and patients with detectable ctDNA had a higher median volume. Agreement was partial, and adding ctDNA early in treatment to volume-based prediction of pathological complete response gave only a numerical gain that was not statistically significant. ctDNA positivity after treatment added significantly to volume for predicting distant recurrence and death. A mismatch calls for checking dates, assay limits, the imaged region and the exact finding. It does not by itself show a false test or hidden metastatic disease.

Controls can be standard care, standard care plus placebo or another protocol-defined option, not automatically no treatment. A fictional single-group Drug A study showing shrinkage supports an activity question for further study; it does not isolate added survival benefit from selection, natural history and other care. A randomized A-plus-usual-care versus usual-care comparison can test the added effect under sound conduct and analysis, while a volunteer cannot choose their randomized assignment or be promised benefit. A chance-assigned two-group phase 2 trial is randomized even though it is not phase 3.

rows.entailment: Imaging reports regional physical findings; the uncontrolled shrinkage example does not isolate added benefit or cause.

evidence.excerpt: A randomized trial assigns eligible consenting participants to interventions by chance. Concealing the next assignment protects enrolment against foreknowledge; blinding concerns awareness after assignment. These are different design features. Randomization reduces treatment-selection confounding but leaves possible chance imbalance, missing outcomes and limits on applicability. The comparator, endpoint, analysis and conduct determine what the comparison establishes.

Concealed chance assignment is different from predictable alternation between A and B. Allocation concealment hides the next assignment during enrolment; blinding concerns who knows the assigned treatment afterwards and may not be feasible for every intervention. Report sequence generation, allocation, who was blinded, assigned-group analyses, exclusions, dropout, missing assessments, treatment changes and unequal follow-up. Chance can balance measured and unmeasured factors on average without guaranteeing identical groups in one trial. Random assignment is not random sampling from a population: consenting eligible volunteers remain selected.

Transcription makes RNA from DNA; translation reads a coding message in codons to make a polypeptide. This information-flow description does not require every RNA to become protein. evidence.excerpt: Recognition differs by subset, and it is not always free of HLA. For the Vγ9Vδ2 subset, which responds to phosphoantigens (small phosphorylated metabolites produced by microbes and overexpressed by some cancers), butyrophilin 2A1 (BTN2A1) binds the Vγ9 chain of the receptor, associates with a second butyrophilin, BTN3A1, and the two act together to start the response; a second ligand, possibly BTN3A1, binds a separate region that includes the Vδ2 chain (Rigau et al., 2020). This is not a peptide sitting in an HLA groove. HLA independence is also not universal: one characterised Vγ5Vδ1 receptor was restricted by HLA-A*24:02 and depended on the CD8-alpha co-receptor, acting on blood-cancer and solid-tumour cells in vitro and in vivo while sparing healthy tissue in those models (Kierkels et al., 2019). That receptor's mechanism is not an eligibility rule for the family.

A typical IgG has two antigen-binding arms; receptor binding and cross-reactivity depend on the particular molecule and test system, while its stem (the Fc region) can recruit immune cells and complement or extend the antibody's life in the blood. Therapeutic antibodies block growth receptors (trastuzumab on HER2, cetuximab on EGFR), release the brakes on T cells (pembrolizumab on PD-1), flag cancer cells for immune killing (rituximab on CD20), or serve as the targeting vehicle of ADCs and radioimmunotherapy. Bispecific formats have two binding specificities. Some are designed to bring a T cell and a target cell together; their structures and functions vary. Fab, the arm with the binding site, and Fc, the stem, are separate parts: binding does not guarantee killing, and Fc effector contacts need compatible effector cells or complement. Antibodies that bind the same target can act differently: a blocking antibody, an antibody-drug conjugate and a bispecific format can share a target and still differ in what follows.

Some inhibitory NK receptors recognize self HLA class I, while activating receptors respond to other features. Reduced self display can weaken an inhibitory input, but the NK cell, its prior education, activating signals and target context still determine the response. NK cells can also contribute antibody-dependent killing through Fc receptors. Donor-derived or engineered NK-cell products need their own compatibility, persistence and safety assessment rather than a blanket claim that matching or rejection never matters. The principle comes from mouse experiments: lymphoma cells selected for loss of H-2 were less malignant at low dose and were rejected by a non-adaptive mechanism, which suggested that natural killer cells are effectors in a defence system geared to detect reduced self MHC (Kärre et al., 1986); that does not guarantee the same outcome for any human tumour. MHC class I molecules are ligands for killer-cell immunoglobulin-like receptors (Parham, 2005): two-domain KIR2D receptors bind HLA-C alleles and three-domain KIR3D receptors bind HLA-A and HLA-B alleles, and the KIR family includes activating as well as inhibitory members (Mariuzza et al., 2025). CD94/NKG2A binds HLA-E, and HLA-E surface expression was enough to protect target cells from lysis by CD94/NKG2A-positive NK clones (Braud et al., 1998). NKG2D binds class I-related proteins including MICA, MICB and ULBP1 to 3 (Mariuzza et al., 2025), and engagement of NKG2D activated NK and gamma-delta T-cell cytolysis against epithelial tumour cells expressing MICA (Bauer et al., 1999). No single activating receptor dominates, since NK cells integrate synergistic signals from several (Long et al., 2013), and responsiveness depends on prior education: in human cell experiments, cytokine stimulation let hyporesponsive NK cells acquire KIR and function when the cognate MHC was present (Juelke et al., 2009). Loss of one HLA allele is not loss of all class I. Loss of beta-2 microglobulin removed surface class I in one of four relapsing melanoma patients (Zaretsky et al., 2016), and because HLA-E is assembled with beta-2 microglobulin, the KIR and NKG2A restraints would be expected to lift together; that last step is an inference not tested in the cited abstracts. A flow-based cytotoxicity assay that stains target and effector nuclei separately and distinguishes live from dead nuclei has been validated with NK-92 cells, CAR-T cells and tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (Rabinovich et al., 2019). Target death is not a count of effector cells that released granule contents: surface CD107a marked NK cells that degranulated after stimulation with MHC-devoid targets and correlated with lysis, and also marked a large subset that did not secrete cytokine, so different readouts count different cells (Alter et al., 2004). CD16 is a low-affinity Fc receptor for IgG that mediates antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity by NK cells (Liu, 2022), a route separate from missing-self recognition. Neither assay readout shows tumour entry or clinical benefit.

For a coding change to supply a conventional T-cell target, its information must be expressed, protein produced and processed into a fragment, that peptide displayed with HLA, and a suitable receptor able to recognise the display. DNA, RNA, protein, recovered displayed peptide and controlled recognition are separate observations. A prediction at one step does not measure all the others. This conventional alpha-beta route does not describe every T cell, antibody or natural killer recognition system.
